newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge defence chief known as torture master.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge defence chief known as torture master.

text.p: Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen, said to have been brutally murdered earlier this week at the hands of his comrades, was known as one of the most treacherous and feared leaders behind Cambodia's "killing fields."

Son Sen, who would have turned 67 on June 12, was murdered by reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot in the pre-dawn hours of June 10 along with his wife and 10 other family members, deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay told a news conference on Saturday.
He produced grisly, enlarged photographs that he said showed the dead bodies of Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen, his wife Yun Yat and other family members.
The photograph said to be of Son Sen showed a bloody corpse, face frozen in a grimace and a bullet hole in the head.
Another showed the crumpled body of what was said to be his wife, Yun Yath, in a pool of blood. Others showed individuals sprawled in the forest, some with deep head wounds.
Son Sen's apparent end appeared to be as horrible and brutal as the deaths of many who suffered under him during the Khmer Rouge's 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime.
As defence minister and deputy prime minister under Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, the stony Son Sen ran the state security aparatus responsible for the deaths of more than one million Cambodians.
Scholars said Tuol Sleng, the former high school that became a torture centre for political opponents, was under his direct responsibility. About 20,000 people were tortured to death there.
Son Sen studied in France during the 1950s with Pol Pot and later returned to Cambodia where he began teaching and becoming active in the communist movement.
He was promoted steadily within the nascent Khmer Rouge movement and commanded the final attack on Phnom Penh that brought the rebels to power in April 1975.

His wife, Yun Yath, also played a prominent role in the Khmer Rouge regime, serving as minister of information and culture and later working to wipe out the Buddhist religion during the rebels' regime.
But despite their prominent role in the Maoist guerrilla movement, their relationship with Pol Pot was strained at times.
Son Sen incurred the wrath of Pol Pot and was relieved of his duties in 1992 when he advocated peace with the government, but was reinstated after he confessed his "mistakes," scholars said.
The Khmer Rouge, who reneged on a 1991 peace pact meant to end Cambodia's long war, have been fighting the coalition government formed following U.N. polls in 1993.
But they have been decimated by thousands of defections since last August, and fewer than 2,000 hard-line fighters are thought to remain.
